title: Tooth anatomy, tissues, and the numbering system
objective: Identify the four dental tissues, name crown and root structures, and assign teeth correct Universal Numbering System numbers.
body:
Almost every Dental Science question assumes you can picture a tooth and name it precisely. Before you study disease or procedures, lock in the vocabulary of structure, tissue, and position.

**The four dental tissues.** A tooth is built from three hard tissues and one soft tissue.
- **Enamel** covers the anatomical crown. It is the hardest substance in the body, about 96 percent mineral (mostly hydroxyapatite), and it has no living cells, so it cannot repair itself once a cavity forms.
- **Dentin** makes up the bulk of the tooth beneath the enamel and cementum. It contains microscopic tubules, which is why exposed dentin feels sensitive to cold.
- **Cementum** is a thin, bonelike layer covering the root. Fibers of the periodontal ligament anchor into it.
- **Pulp** is the soft tissue in the center, containing nerves and blood vessels. The pulp chamber sits in the crown and continues as root canals that open at the **apex** through the apical foramen.

**Crown, root, and supporting structures.** The **cementoenamel junction (CEJ)** is the line where enamel meets cementum, dividing anatomical crown from root. The tooth sits in a socket of alveolar bone, suspended by the **periodontal ligament**, and is surrounded by **gingiva**. Together these supporting tissues are called the periodontium.

**Tooth types and dentitions.** Incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars grind. Adults have 32 permanent teeth; children have 20 primary teeth, with no premolars and no third molars.

**The Universal Numbering System.** Used in most U.S. dental offices, it numbers permanent teeth 1 through 32. Start with the patient's maxillary right third molar as #1, move across the upper arch to the maxillary left third molar (#16), drop to the mandibular left third molar (#17), and continue across to the mandibular right third molar (#32). Primary teeth use capital letters A through T in the same clockwise path. Remember that the chart is written from the patient's point of view, not yours.

**Surfaces.** Each tooth has named surfaces: mesial (toward the midline), distal (away from it), facial (buccal on posterior teeth, labial on anterior teeth), lingual (toward the tongue; palatal on maxillary teeth), and occlusal on posterior teeth or the incisal edge on anterior teeth. A cavity touching mesial and occlusal surfaces is charted as an MO lesion.

The most common mistake is charting from the operator's point of view. When you face a patient, their right side is on your left, so students who number from their own left mislabel every tooth by arch side, turning #3 into #14.
examples: Tooth #8 is the patient's maxillary right central incisor, and #9 is the maxillary left central incisor right beside it.
A five-year-old's lower left second primary molar is charted as K, because primary teeth use letters A through T.
Cold water causes a sharp twinge where gum recession has exposed root dentin, because fluid moves in the open dentinal tubules.

questions.stem: A dental assistant charts a filling in a patient's maxillary left first molar using the Universal Numbering System. Which number should she record?
questions.explanation: Counting from #1 (maxillary right third molar) across the upper arch, the maxillary left first molar is #14. #3 is the maxillary right first molar, the error made when charting from the operator's own side.

questions.stem: Which tissue cannot repair itself after a carious lesion breaks through it, because it contains no living cells?
questions.explanation: Mature enamel has no cells, so lost enamel is not regenerated. Dentin is the tempting choice, but living odontoblasts can lay down reparative dentin.

questions.stem: A patient's root surface is exposed by gum recession. Which tissue covers the root and provides attachment for periodontal ligament fibers?
questions.explanation: Cementum covers the root and anchors the periodontal ligament fibers. Enamel covers only the anatomical crown, not the root.

questions.stem: A dentist notes decay on the surface of tooth #29 that faces the tongue. Which surface is that?
questions.explanation: The lingual surface faces the tongue. Facial faces the lips or cheeks, the opposite side, so it is the main distractor.

questions.stem: How many teeth make up a complete primary dentition?
questions.explanation: There are 20 primary teeth: incisors, canines, and molars in each quadrant, with no premolars. 32 is the full permanent dentition, including third molars.

questions.stem: A radiograph shows an infection at the tip of a root, where vessels and nerves enter the tooth. What is this location called?
questions.explanation: The apex is the root tip where the apical foramen admits nerves and vessels. The CEJ is where crown meets root near the gumline, not at the root tip.

questions.stem: A cavity involves the surface of a premolar that faces the midline and its chewing surface. How is it recorded?
questions.explanation: Mesial faces toward the midline and occlusal is the chewing surface, so the lesion is MO. DO would mean the surface facing away from the midline.

questions.stem: Which structure suspends a tooth in its socket and helps cushion chewing forces?
questions.explanation: The periodontal ligament connects cementum to alveolar bone and absorbs chewing forces. Gingiva surrounds the neck of the tooth but does not anchor it to bone.

flashcards.definition: Hardest tissue in the body, about 96 percent mineral, covering the anatomical crown; it has no living cells and cannot repair itself.
Tissue forming the bulk of the tooth under enamel and cementum, containing tubules that transmit sensation.
The line where enamel meets cementum, dividing the anatomical crown from the root.
U.S. system numbering permanent teeth 1 to 32 starting at the patient's maxillary right third molar; primary teeth are lettered A to T.
Fibrous tissue that anchors the cementum to alveolar bone and cushions chewing forces.
